title: Forty Seconds and the Loop
book: Boyd: The Fighter Pilot Who Changed the Art of War
author: Robert Coram
wiifm: Speed is not just about moving fast. It is about seeing, deciding and acting faster than the other side can adjust. John Boyd was a brash American fighter pilot who turned that idea into the OODA loop, observe, orient, decide, act, now used in boardrooms, hospitals and police training. Robert Coram's biography follows a poor boy from Erie, Pennsylvania, who beat every challenger in forty seconds, reinvented how fighter planes were judged, and fought his own air force from the inside. Coram admires him openly, so we will keep an eye on the legend too.

ch.h: A boy by a frozen lake
b: John Richard Boyd was born on 23 January 1927 in Erie, Pennsylvania, a grey industrial town on the shore of Lake Erie. When he was three, his father died of pneumonia, leaving his mother, Elsie, to raise five children through the Great Depression. Money was desperately short. Coram describes a proud, strict mother who drilled into her children that they were as good as anyone and must never be pitied.

Boyd grew up tough, loud and competitive. He became a strong swimmer, training in the cold waters of Lake Erie, and swimming taught him something he would use for life: a race can be won by small advantages in how quickly you turn and change direction, not just by raw speed.

He enlisted in the Army Air Forces in 1944, near the end of the Second World War, and served in occupied Japan as a swimming instructor. He then went to the University of Iowa on the GI Bill, studied economics, joined the reserve officer programme, and was commissioned into the new United States Air Force in 1951. He wanted one thing: to fly fighters.
ch.cap: Young John Boyd dives into grey, choppy Lake Erie

b: Boyd trained as a fighter pilot and reached Korea in 1953, flying the F-86 Sabre, though the war ended before he shot down any enemy aircraft. Then he was sent to the Fighter Weapons School at Nellis Air Force Base in Nevada, first as a student and then as an instructor.

Korea gave him a puzzle he would chew on for years. In the skies over the north, in what pilots called MiG Alley, the American F-86 Sabre was shooting down Soviet-built MiG-15s at a striking rate, often claimed at around ten to one, though later research has cut that figure sharply. On paper the MiG was the better aircraft: it could climb faster, turn tighter at height and fly higher. So why did the Sabre win? Boyd eventually concluded that the Sabre had two quiet advantages. Its bubble canopy let the pilot see more, and its hydraulic controls let him switch from one manoeuvre to the next more quickly. The Sabre pilot could change what he was doing faster than the MiG pilot could respond.

At Nellis he made his name. He offered a standing bet to any pilot: start with your aircraft on his tail, in a position of advantage, and he would reverse the situation and be on your tail within forty seconds, or pay forty dollars. The story goes that he never lost. Pilots called him Forty-Second Boyd. Coram reports that the record was unbroken, though as with many legends, it rests largely on the memories of men who flew with him.

He was also loud, profane, rude to superiors, and given to jabbing a finger into people's chests as he argued, sometimes burning holes in their ties with his cigar. Coram calls him a warrior in the purest sense, but plenty of officers simply found him impossible.

In 1959 he wrote the Aerial Attack Study, a manual that for the first time set out air-to-air combat tactics systematically, describing every manoeuvre and its counter. It became the basis of fighter tactics for the US Air Force and later other air forces. He was thirty-two.
ch.cap: Forty-second Boyd swings onto his challenger's tail

b: Boyd realised he did not understand the physics of why his manoeuvres worked. So he went back to school, taking a degree in industrial engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology, which he completed in 1962. Studying thermodynamics, he had a flash of insight.

A fighter in combat is constantly trading energy: height, which is stored energy, for speed, which is moving energy, and back again. The plane that can gain energy faster, or lose it more slowly in a tight turn, can out-manoeuvre the other. He called this energy-manoeuvrability theory, and with a mathematician named Thomas Christie he worked out how to measure it for any aircraft.

In plain terms, the key number was what engineers call specific excess power: how much energy an aircraft can gain or lose at a given speed, height and load. Plot it across every combination, and you can compare two aircraft at a glance, seeing exactly where one beats the other. A pilot could use those charts to fight only where his aircraft had the edge, and a designer could use them to decide what a new aircraft really needed.

To run the calculations he needed huge amounts of computer time, which he did not have permission to use. According to Coram, he and Christie used it anyway, logging the work under other projects, and Boyd was investigated for the theft of computer time. The case was dropped once it became clear how valuable the results were.

The charts were devastating. They showed that American fighters were worse than Soviet fighters in large parts of the flight envelope. It was the first of many times Boyd would take on his own institution with numbers it could not argue with.
ch.cap: Boyd feeds punch cards to a borrowed mainframe at night

b: In the mid 1960s Boyd was sent to the Pentagon to help design a new fighter, the F-X. The original concept was a huge, heavy, complicated aircraft. Using his energy charts, Boyd argued for something lighter and more agile. The result, after long battles, was the F-15 Eagle.

He then joined a small group of reformers, nicknamed the fighter mafia, including Pierre Sprey and the test pilot Everest Riccioni. Working partly behind the backs of senior officers, they pushed for a lightweight fighter that would be cheap, nimble and good at dogfighting. That project led to the F-16 Fighting Falcon, and a parallel design became the basis of the navy's F/A-18 Hornet.

Coram presents Boyd as the near single-handed father of these aircraft. Other historians give more credit to engineers and officials such as Harry Hillaker at General Dynamics and the Pentagon analysts who supported the programme. The fair summary is that Boyd's theory and stubbornness were essential, but he was part of a team.

There was also a spell in Asia. In 1972 and 1973, near the end of the Vietnam War, Boyd served at Nakhon Phanom air base in Thailand, where he ran a secretive operation monitoring sensors along the Ho Chi Minh Trail. Coram uses the posting to show his reputation for integrity: he is said to have refused perks and pushed back against waste. It was his last major field assignment.

Coram tells a story about Boyd's advice to young officers, a choice between two roads. You can be somebody, get promoted and go along with the system. Or you can do something, make a real difference, and probably pay for it. To be or to do, which way will you go? Boyd chose to do. He retired as a colonel in 1975, never promoted to general.
ch.cap: Boyd jabs a finger at the lightweight fighter drawing

b: Retirement freed him to think about something bigger than aeroplanes. He lived simply, in a small apartment in Arlington, Virginia, on his pension, and he read enormously: history, physics, biology, philosophy, Sun Tzu, Clausewitz, Liddell Hart, the German blitzkrieg.

In 1976 he wrote a short paper called Destruction and Creation. It is about how we understand the world. We build mental models, he argued, but reality keeps changing, and any model eventually stops matching it. He drew on Gödel's incompleteness theorem, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and the second law of thermodynamics to argue that a closed system of thought becomes increasingly confused.

Think of it this way. Imagine taking apart a skier, a motorboat, a bicycle and a tank. From the skis, the outboard motor, the handlebars and the caterpillar tracks you could build something new: a snowmobile. Boyd used exactly this example. Breaking down what you know into parts frees you from old categories, and recombining the parts lets you make something that fits the world as it now is.

The answer is a constant cycle. First you smash your existing ideas into pieces, which he called destructive deduction. Then you combine the pieces in new ways to form a better model, which he called creative induction. Then reality moves again, and you repeat. Some scientists have pointed out that his use of Gödel and Heisenberg is more metaphor than physics, but the core idea, that your picture of the world must keep being rebuilt, is the foundation for everything that follows.
ch.cap: Skis, motor, handlebars and tracks become a snowmobile

b: From these ideas grew the concept Boyd is famous for, the OODA loop. Observe, orient, decide, act. Every person and every organisation in a contest goes round this cycle continuously. You take in what is happening, make sense of it, choose what to do, and do it, which changes the situation, which you must observe again.

Boyd's insight was that if you go round the loop faster than your opponent, and more importantly if you can get inside his loop, he will always be reacting to a situation that has already changed. His actions become irrelevant, then confused, then panicky. Eventually he collapses, not because he has been physically destroyed but because his picture of the world no longer fits reality.

Boyd gave the idea a more precise vocabulary. What really mattered, he argued, were fast transients: the speed at which you can shift from one action to another, just like the Sabre pilot over Korea. And the purpose of operating at that tempo was to generate in the enemy what he called menace, uncertainty and mistrust, until the opponent's organisation pulled itself apart. You do not simply outfight the other side. You make them lose confidence in their own picture of reality.

Here is something often missed. Boyd thought orientation was the most important step. It is where your culture, experience, training and assumptions shape what you even notice. His later diagrams show orientation feeding back to every other step. A fast loop with poor orientation just makes mistakes quickly. The real advantage comes from seeing more clearly than the other side, and then acting on it quickly.

This is also why he valued trust and decentralised command. If people on the ground understand the intent and trust each other, they can act without waiting for orders from the top, so the whole organisation cycles faster.
ch.cap: Observe, orient, decide, act: the loop spins faster

b: Boyd never wrote a book. Instead he built a briefing called Patterns of Conflict, a stack of slides that grew to almost two hundred pages and took up to fourteen hours to deliver. He would only give it in full. Officers, congressmen and journalists sat through it, sometimes over two days.

In it he tracked conflict from Sun Tzu to the present and argued that the winners had used what came to be called manoeuvre warfare: speed, surprise, ambiguity and decentralised initiative, aimed at shattering the enemy's cohesion rather than grinding down his forces. He drew heavily on the German blitzkrieg and on the indirect approach you heard yesterday.

His audience grew in the early 1980s with what became known as the military reform movement. Members of Congress, including Senator Gary Hart, formed a Military Reform Caucus to question expensive, complex weapons and attritional thinking. The journalist James Fallows drew on Boyd and his circle in his 1981 book National Defense. For a while the restless colonel in the small Arlington flat was one of the most talked about thinkers in Washington.

His influence on the United States Marine Corps was especially strong. In 1989 the Marines adopted a doctrine manual, Warfighting, built around manoeuvre warfare. Coram credits Boyd as its key intellectual source, a view the Marine authors themselves have broadly acknowledged.

Coram's most dramatic claim is that Boyd's ideas shaped the plan for the 1991 Gulf War, when the Defense Secretary Dick Cheney, who had attended Boyd's briefings, pushed for a sweeping move around the Iraqi flank. This is debated. Some historians think Coram overstates Boyd's direct role, since the left hook was developed by army planners using existing doctrine.

He kept expanding the work. Further briefings followed, with titles like Organic Design for Command and Control, The Strategic Game of Interaction and Isolation, and finally, in 1995, a short summary called The Essence of Winning and Losing, which contains his fullest drawing of the OODA loop. He never turned any of it into a book, which is partly why his ideas are so often reduced to a slogan.
ch.cap: Boyd's briefing runs on, slide after slide, for hours

b: Coram does not hide the cost of Boyd's choices. He was often absent and harsh at home. His wife, Mary, raised five children largely on her own, on a modest income, and several of his children later spoke of a distant and difficult father. The man who could see inside an enemy's decision cycle was not always good at seeing the people closest to him.

In his last years Boyd developed prostate cancer. He moved to Florida, and he died on 9 March 1997, aged seventy. He was buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Coram records that the Marine Corps sent a strong representation to the funeral, while the Air Force, the service he had fought for and argued with, was barely present. The Marines later placed his papers in their research centre at Quantico.

Robert Coram, a journalist and novelist, published the biography in 2002, drawing on interviews with Boyd's friends, family and colleagues. It is affectionate and partisan, and Coram makes Boyd into a hero who was almost always right. Later scholars, such as Frans Osinga, have given a more careful account of his thought.

Since then the loop has escaped the military entirely. Business writers, among them Boyd's friend Chet Richards in his 2004 book Certain to Win, applied it to companies competing in fast markets. Emergency medicine, cyber security and police training use versions of it. Many of these borrowings flatten it into a simple four-step circle, which Boyd would have hated. His point was never just speed. It was speed built on better orientation.

But the core of what Boyd taught holds up. Keep rebuilding your picture of the world. Orient well, then cycle faster than the other side. Trust your people with your intent so they can act without waiting. And remember the choice he offered to every young officer he mentored: to be somebody, or to do something.
ch.cap: Marines honour Boyd at Arlington as the sun rises

take: Boyd said orientation, how you make sense of what you see, is the heart of the loop. Regularly question the assumptions shaping how your team reads the market.
If you observe, decide and act faster, competitors end up reacting to a world that has already moved. Shorten the time between seeing a problem and doing something about it.
Destruction and Creation argued every mental model goes stale. Every few months, take your business plan apart and ask what reality now looks like.
Decentralised action only works if people understand the intent and trust each other. Tell staff what you are trying to achieve, then let them decide how.
Use numbers to beat the institution
Boyd's energy charts won arguments that opinion could not. When you challenge the way things are done, bring data nobody can dismiss.
The fighter mafia preferred cheap, agile aircraft over expensive, complex ones. A lean, nimble offer can beat a bloated one.
You can chase status or chase results, and sometimes you cannot have both. Decide which matters more before the choice arrives.
Boyd's devotion to his work came at a heavy price for his family. Speed and conviction at work need balancing with the people who depend on you.
recall: What are the four stages of the OODA loop?

Observe, orient, decide and act. Each contestant cycles through them continuously, and the aim is to cycle faster and more accurately than the opponent so he is always reacting to an outdated picture.
Why did Boyd consider orientation the most important step?
Because culture, experience and assumptions shape what you notice and how you interpret it. A fast loop with poor orientation only produces fast mistakes.

Boyd's insight that air combat is a trade of height and speed, both forms of energy, and that an aircraft's ability to gain or keep energy can be measured. It showed American fighters' weaknesses and shaped the F-15 and F-16.
Boyd offered to start with an opponent on his tail and reverse the position within forty seconds, or pay forty dollars. Legend says he never lost.
What was Destruction and Creation about?
A 1976 paper arguing that mental models become outdated as reality changes, so we must break them down and recombine the parts into new, better models, again and again.
note: Coram's 2002 biography is based on interviews and is openly admiring; Frans Osinga's Science, Strategy and War (2007) gives a more scholarly account of Boyd's ideas. The forty-second record, the computer-time episode and Boyd's role in the F-16 and in the 1991 Gulf War plan come largely from Coram and those who knew Boyd, and other historians give more credit to engineers and army planners. Boyd's influence on the Marine Corps manual Warfighting (1989) is well documented.
words: A person who attacks cherished beliefs or established institutions.
Boyd was an iconoclast inside his own air force, using energy charts to show that its prized fighters were worse than Soviet ones across much of the flight envelope.
A brief, passing state, or the shift from one state to another.
Boyd's fast transients were the speed with which a pilot could switch from one manoeuvre to the next, the hidden edge of the Sabre over the MiG.
A measure of disorder, which in a closed system tends to increase over time.
In Destruction and Creation Boyd borrowed entropy as a metaphor: a closed system of thought grows ever more confused unless it is broken apart and rebuilt.
Combining separate parts or ideas into a new whole.
Boyd's snowmobile, built in the mind from skis, an outboard motor, handlebars and tank tracks, is his picture of synthesis, which he called creative induction.
Strongly and openly favouring one side or person.
Coram's biography is affectionate and partisan, so scholars such as Frans Osinga are the better guide to what Boyd's ideas actually were.

Down one path, you can be somebody: go along with the system, make the right friends, and get promoted. biz: Get inside the enquiry loop, without rushing the customer

Homeowners enquiring about secured loans often contact several brokers, so the firm that reaches them first, and makes sense of their situation first, usually wins. Set a target this week for first contact within five minutes in opening hours, with an instant WhatsApp acknowledgement out of hours. But Boyd's real lesson is orientation: open each call by understanding why the customer is borrowing and whether a secured loan is even suitable, not by pitching. Speed to contact, never speed to decision; customers should always have time to think. Measure contact rate, conversion and complaints by speed band to see what the extra minutes are worth.
Write the commander's intent for your team

Boyd valued decentralised command: if people understand the intent and trust each other, they act without waiting for orders. Write one short page for staff on both brands. For HomeownersLoan: find each customer a suitable outcome, even if that outcome is no loan. For Debt Support Direct: if a client shows signs of vulnerability or crisis, slow down, record it, and adapt the support before anything else. Then give staff authority to act on it. Each month, run a destruction and creation review: list three assumptions about what works, test them against the data, and rebuild. Measure vulnerability flags recorded and good outcomes.
connects: The loop of observe, orient, decide and act is a feedback loop, and Meadows explains why delays in such loops make whole systems overshoot and collapse, which is what Boyd tried to inflict on enemies.
Dalio's habit of reflecting on pain to rebuild his model of reality echoes Boyd's Destruction and Creation, where every mental picture must be smashed and remade as the world changes.
Boyd read Sun Tzu closely and built on his idea that the decisive battle is fought in the opponent's mind, aiming to make the enemy's picture of reality stop fitting the facts.
recap:
John Boyd was born in nineteen twenty-seven in Erie, Pennsylvania, a grey industrial town on a cold lake. When he was three his father died, and his mother raised five children through the Great Depression, telling them they were as good as anyone. Boyd grew up loud, tough and competitive, and swimming taught him that races are won by how fast you turn, not just how fast you go.

He became a fighter pilot and an instructor at the Fighter Weapons School in Nevada, where he offered every pilot a bet. Start on his tail, and in forty seconds he would be on yours. The story goes that he never lost. They called him Forty-Second Boyd.

His first big idea came from a puzzle over Korea. The Soviet jet was better on paper, yet the American Sabre kept winning. Boyd decided the Sabre pilot could see more, and switch from one manoeuvre to the next more quickly. The winner was the one who could change faster.

His second idea came from physics. Studying engineering, he realised air combat is a constant trade of height for speed and back again, and with a mathematician he measured it for any aircraft. The charts showed that American fighters were worse than Soviet ones in large areas of combat. He was investigated for using computer time without permission, and the case was dropped once the results proved valuable. He went on to help shape two of the most successful fighters ever built.

His third idea was about thinking itself. In retirement, in a small flat near Washington, he argued that every mental model of the world eventually stops fitting reality, so you must keep breaking your ideas apart and recombining them into something new.

From that came the fourth and most famous idea, the loop: observe, orient, decide, act. Cycle faster than your opponent, get inside his loop, and he is always reacting to a world that has already changed, until he loses confidence in his own picture of reality. But Boyd insisted that orientation matters most. A fast loop built on poor understanding just makes mistakes quickly.

The fifth idea was trust. People who understand the intent can act without waiting for orders, so the whole organisation moves faster. The Marine Corps built its doctrine on his thinking.

He paid for his choices, at home and in his career, and retired a colonel. He died in nineteen ninety-seven.

The line to remember: see more clearly, then change faster, and choose to do something rather than to be somebody.
